definition: Terrestrial means relating to or living on land, as opposed to in water or in the air.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word terrestrial. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know terrestrial should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Kiwis are among the most thoroughly terrestrial of all birds, nesting and feeding entirely on the forest floor.
Land-based describes where an operation or force is stationed -- land-based missiles, a land-based air fleet -- rather than where a creature naturally lives, which is the claim terrestrial makes.
Land-bound is stronger, suggesting an animal cannot leave the land at all, while a terrestrial animal may still swim a river or climb a tree from time to time.

Land-dwelling states where an animal makes its home and nothing more. Terrestrial says that of animals too, but stretches much further -- terrestrial ecosystems, terrestrial planets, terrestrial broadcasting -- wherever land or the ground itself is the point.

Ground-based describes equipment and operations run from the ground rather than from the air or from orbit -- a ground-based telescope, ground-based radar. Terrestrial is the naturalist's word for life that belongs to land rather than to water or the air.

A zoologist sorting a museum's snail drawers applies one simple test: does the animal breathe with a lung or with a gill?
The lunged snails cannot breathe under water at all, and they crawl over leaf litter, seal themselves against dry weather, and drown if held under for long.
The gilled ones cannot survive a single day out of the pond.
The lunged half of the collection goes into a drawer labelled terrestrial.
Snails that breathe air, crawl over leaf litter, and drown if held under water belong entirely to the land, and terrestrial is the word for land-living.

Terrestrial contrasts with life in water and life in the air, and in broadcasting it means transmitted from the ground rather than by satellite.
Its water-side counterpart in this unit is aquatic, and an animal that genuinely divides its life between the two is neither one nor the other but amphibious.

For some three billion years, every living thing on Earth stayed in the water.
The move ashore began small: algal mats at the tide line, then mosses, then millipede-like creatures that could manage brief trips between pools.
Becoming truly terrestrial demanded more than a way to breathe air.
An animal on land must carry its own moisture, hold its body up without water's support, and lay eggs that will not dry out.
Fossil trackways in Scotland record one of the earliest animals to manage it fully, an arthropod that fed and bred out of the water entirely.
Every forest, desert and grassland that followed stands on that first slow crossing of the shore.
